Paper_name: Does Self-Associating a Geometric Shape Immediately Cause Attentional Prioritization? Comparing Familiar Versus Recently Self-Associated Stimuli in the Dot-Probe Task
Summary: This research disentangled the potential of self- versus stranger-representations for familiar, new, and paired (familiar + new) stimuli to guide attention, combining the self-matching task (Sui et al., 2012) as a manipulation check with a dot-probe task. In Study 1 (N = 34 analyzed), familiar and new self- versus stranger representations were tested in a dot-probe task with a short SOA (100 ms); Studies 2 (N = 31) and 3 (N = 35 reported; 34 analyzed per participants section) used a long SOA (1,000 ms) to test inhibition of return. Significant performance differences for targets following self- versus stranger-associated stimuli (cueing effect or IOR depending on SOA) were observed only when familiar representations were present: under conditions of attentional competition, familiar self-representations impact the distribution of attention while new self-representations alone do not. In all three studies the matching task showed a significant self-prioritization effect (faster responses for matching self-associated shape-label pairs), confirming successful shape-label association.
Author: Gabriela Orellana-Corrales, Christina Matschke, Ann-Katrin Wesslein
Conclusion: Familiar self-representations (labels and shape-label pairs) guide attention more efficiently than stranger representations in a dot-probe task, whereas newly self-associated geometric shapes alone do not; the matching task confirmed a robust SPE (faster and more accurate responses for matching self-associated shape-label pairs) in all three studies.
